transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello, Dr. [Name]. I, um, I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten completely out of hand, and I don't really know how to stop it anymore. It's embarrassing to even talk about, honestly, especially at my age. You'd think a 54-year-old woman who manages a whole office full of administrative staff would have some self-control, right? But I just... I keep having these evenings, usually after work when the office has been a madhouse, and I'll stop on the way home and order takeout. But not just a regular meal for one. I'm talking about a whole family-size order, like enough to feed four people. And then, as if that wasn't enough, I'll run into the grocery store next door and grab bags of chips, or maybe those big bakery muffins or a whole cake. And I tell myself I'm just getting it for the week, you know, just stocking up. But then I get home, and I sit down, and I just start eating. And I eat, and I eat, and it's like I'm not even fully there. I'll eat almost all of it myself before I even seem to register how much is actually gone. It's like I blink, and all these empty containers and wrappers are just sitting there staring back at me.

Can you describe what you mean by 'it's like I blink, and all these empty containers and wrappers are just sitting there staring back at me'? Were you aware of eating that much as it was happening, or did it feel like you were out of control?

Out of control is... well, it is exactly that. It's just exactly that. Which is so deeply frustrating because, like I was saying before, I manage people for a living! I make executive decisions all day long, I put out fires, I tell people what to do. But sitting there at my kitchen island with all that food, it is like... well, once I start, there is just this awful switch that flips. It really is like a physical switch in my brain has been thrown. 

I will actually be sitting there, and I can hear my own voice in my head, plain as day, thinking, Taylor, put it away. Taylor, you have had enough, just wrap it up and put it in the fridge. I am literally begging myself to stop. But... but my hands, they just keep going. They just keep reaching and opening containers, ripping into the plastic, pulling out another piece of whatever it is I bought. It is like I am not the one in charge of my own body anymore. I am just watching my hands do it, totally disconnected from the action. 

I'll be chewing and swallowing, and my mind is screaming to stop, but the hands just keep moving from the bag to my mouth, over and over, opening another box, peeling another wrapper. It is the most terrifying, helpless feeling in the world, to be trapped inside yourself while your body does something you desperately want it to stop doing. I just... I can't seem to make the connection between my brain saying stop and my hands actually stopping, no matter how hard I try to reason with myself in the moment.
After these episodes of eating, do you ever try to compensate for the food you’ve eaten, such as by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

No, no, I don't do anything like that. I know some people do, you know, you read about it in magazines or see it on those daytime talk shows, where people make themselves sick or they run on the treadmill for five hours straight. But I don't do any of that. I've never made myself throw up, not once. The very thought of it just... well, it makes me shudder, honestly. I've always hated throwing up, ever since I was a little girl and had the stomach flu. And laxatives, no, I don't touch those either. My mother used to use them all the time when I was growing up, always complaining about her digestion, and I just remember thinking how miserable she seemed. 

And as for exercise... well, I'd like to say I exercise, I really would. Every January I tell myself this is the year I'm going to start walking in the mornings before work, or maybe join that water aerobics class at the Y down the street. But by the time I get home from the office, after dealing with all the scheduling conflicts and the payroll issues and whatever crisis the receptionist has managed to create that day, I am just so completely drained. I barely have the energy to walk from my car to the front door, let alone get on a treadmill or go for a run. 

So, no, after it happens... after I eat all that food and the wrappers are just sitting there, I don't try to get rid of it. I just sit there feeling... well, feeling like a complete failure. I just sit with this awful, heavy feeling in my stomach, like a rock, and this overwhelming sense of guilt and shame. I usually just end up dragging myself to bed, feeling absolutely miserable and bloated, and I just lie there thinking about what I've done, promising myself that tomorrow will be different. But I don't do anything to, you know, undo it. I just suffer through the aftermath.
How often do these episodes happen? Are they happening on a regular basis, like once a week or more frequently?

Well, it's funny you ask about the exact timing, because I actually... I keep a journal. Not a diary, really, not like a teenager would keep with a little lock and key, but just a plain little blue notebook I keep on my nightstand. I originally started it because I thought maybe if I wrote down my daily tasks at the office—you know, keeping track of the admin team's PTO requests and the vendor supply orders and all the little things that buzz around in my head—it would help me leave work at work. Just to clear my mind before sleep. 

But then, over time, I started jotting down these... well, these bad evenings. I felt like I needed to keep track of it, maybe to prove to myself that it wasn't happening as often as it felt like it was. But it backfired, really. Because when I look back through my journal now, it’s just... it’s really hard to look at, honestly. There has barely been a week in the last several months without at least one of these nights. Not one week where I just went home and ate a normal dinner. 

And, if I'm being completely truthful with you, saying once a week is letting myself off easy. Most weeks, it happens several times. Like, it might happen on a Tuesday because our payroll software crashed and everyone was panicking, and then it'll happen again on Thursday because two of my clerks called out sick and I had to cover the front desk on top of my own duties. And before I know it, I've had three or four of these massive takeout-and-grocery runs in a single week. 

I'll just flip through the pages of that little notebook, and it’s just entry after entry. You’d think seeing it written down in black and white like that would be a wake-up call, wouldn't you? Like, 'Taylor, look at this, you're doing it three days a week, you have to stop.' But it doesn't stop it. It just documents it. So, yes, it's very regular. Several times a week, for months now, just like clockwork.
Do these episodes of eating cause you significant distress, such as feeling upset, ashamed, or guilty, or interfere with your daily life, like your work or relationships?

Distress... oh, doctor, distress doesn't even begin to cover it. The guilt is just... well, it's completely overwhelming. It eats me alive, honestly. I mean, I wake up the next morning and I have to put on my blazer and my nice shoes and go into the office and pretend to be this completely put-together supervisor who has everything under control, when really, inside, I'm just drowning in this... this immense shame from the night before. 

And it absolutely bleeds into my personal life. It's practically ruined it, if I'm being perfectly honest. I used to be quite social, you know? I loved having my neighbors over for a glass of wine on the patio, or hosting a little weekend brunch for some of the women I used to work with at my old firm. I always prided myself on being a good hostess. But now? I have completely stopped inviting people over. Completely. I can't bear the thought of anyone coming inside my house. Half the time I'm terrified I forgot to take out the trash and they'll see all the takeout bags and empty wrappers stuffed down in the bin, or I'm worried they'll look at me and just... know. Like they can see the failure written all over my face. So I just isolate myself. I make excuses. 

And my evenings... well, I used to have these lovely little evening routines that really helped me unwind after managing the office all day. I used to do a little bit of yoga in the living room—just following along with a DVD I bought years ago, nothing too strenuous, just some stretching to help my back after sitting at a desk and hunching over spreadsheets. Or I would go out back and do some gardening chores. I have these beautiful hydrangeas and a little vegetable patch, and I used to love going out there at dusk to weed or water the tomatoes. It was my quiet time. It was peaceful. 

But now... now, I skip all of that. I haven't unrolled my yoga mat in months, and the weeds are just taking over the garden, which breaks my heart to look at. But I just can't bring myself to do it, because after one of these episodes, I feel too ashamed and preoccupied. I am just so physically uncomfortable and so mentally consumed by what I've just done. I just sit there on the couch, completely paralyzed by the shame of it all, obsessing over the fact that I promised myself I wouldn't do it again, and yet I did. I don't have the emotional energy to stretch or pull weeds or talk to a friend. I just hide away. So, yes, it interferes with everything. My whole life outside of work has just shrunk down to absolutely nothing because of this.
Do you ever experience this same sense of your body acting on its own or being out of control in any other situations, or does it only happen during these eating episodes?

No, no, it really is just the eating. And I think that's what makes it so incredibly frustrating for me, because in every other aspect of my life, I am very much in control. I mean, I have to be, right? As a supervisor, I’m the one everyone comes to when things fall apart. I direct the administrative staff, I handle the disputes, I make sure the office doesn't completely collapse in on itself. If someone is panicking, I am the calm one. I never lose my head, I never just act on impulse or do things without thinking them through first. I am very grounded. 

But with the food... it’s like I become a completely different person. It is strictly limited to those evenings alone in my kitchen. Once I start, there is this awful switch that flips. It's the strangest, most terrifying feeling, honestly. I can literally be sitting there, staring at the counter, and my rational brain is still working—I'll be thinking, *Taylor, put it away. Just close the box, put the lid back on, walk away right now.* I am fully aware that I need to stop. 

But my hands... it's like they belong to someone else entirely. They just keep moving. They just keep opening containers and tearing into packages and pulling things out of bags, like I am not the one in charge at all. I'll just be sitting there, practically watching my own hands do this, feeling completely disconnected from my own physical movements. It’s so bizarre because I don't lose control like that anywhere else. Not when I'm dealing with a furious vendor on the phone, not when I'm driving in terrible traffic, nowhere. It is only ever in those moments with the food, where that switch flips and I am suddenly just a passenger in my own body.
During these episodes, even though you feel out of control, do you feel like you could stop if you really tried, or does it feel like you physically can't stop yourself once you start?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago about that awful switch flipping... it really feels like a physical impossibility to stop. You ask if I could stop if I really tried, and, doctor, I do try. I try so incredibly hard. I sit there at the kitchen island, and I am practically screaming at myself in my own head. I will be sitting there thinking, Taylor, put it away, just stop right now, you know exactly how you're going to feel tomorrow morning when your alarm goes off. 

But it is exactly like I was just trying to explain—my hands just keep opening the containers anyway. It is like there is a complete and total disconnect between my brain and my body. I will be holding one of those plastic takeout boxes, maybe the lo mein or the dumplings from the place down the street, and my rational mind is saying to put it in the fridge and walk away, but my fingers are already prying the lid off. 

It is terrifying, honestly. Because I am trying, I really am trying with every ounce of willpower I have left after a long day at the office, but it is like my body is completely overridden. I am just not the one in charge anymore once that first bite happens. I physically cannot make my hands stop bringing the food to my mouth or tearing open the next package, no matter how much I am begging myself to just put it away. It is just this relentless momentum, and I just have to ride it out until the food is gone, because I absolutely cannot stop myself once it starts.
Outside of these eating episodes, have you ever experienced any other moments where you felt disconnected from yourself or like you were not in control of your body?

No, no, never. I know I sort of just touched on this, but it really is exclusively with the food. You would think if someone has this... this bizarre disconnect, it would happen in other stressful situations, right? But I don't have that at all. 

Like, just last Tuesday at the office, we had this massive crisis. Our main scheduling software went down right before a huge quarterly deadline, and my entire administrative team was in a total panic. I mean, people were practically running around like chickens with their heads cut off, some of the newer girls were practically in tears. And me? I was completely anchored. I just stood there in the middle of the bullpen, took a deep breath, and started delegating. I felt every bit in my body, completely present, totally in control of my actions and my words. I didn't freeze, I didn't feel like I was floating away or watching someone else do my job, like I do with the food. I was right there, handling it, just like I always do. 

I've been managing offices for years, and you just can't afford to lose yourself or disconnect when people are relying on you to keep the operations running smoothly. So, no, I've never experienced anything even remotely like that outside of my house. Everywhere else, I'm just regular, dependable, in-control Taylor. It is literally only when I have those wrappers and containers in front of me that I lose myself. So, to answer your question, no, absolutely not. Just the eating.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a sense of lack of control only during eating episodes or also in other areas of life.
doctor.question: Do you ever experience this same sense of your body acting on its own or being out of control in any other situations, or does it only happen during these eating episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start, there is this awful switch that flips where I can be thinking, Taylor, put it away, and my hands still keep opening containers like I am not the one in charge.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the feeling of being out of control or the body acting on its own, which directly maps to the 'Loss of Control' symptom regarding the eating episodes.

patient.answer:
No, no, it really is just the eating. And I think that's what makes it so incredibly frustrating for me, because in every other aspect of my life, I am very much in control. I mean, I have to be, right? As a supervisor, I’m the one everyone comes to when things fall apart. I direct the administrative staff, I handle the disputes, I make sure the office doesn't completely collapse in on itself. If someone is panicking, I am the calm one. I never lose my head, I never just act on impulse or do things without thinking them through first. I am very grounded. 

But with the food... it’s like I become a completely different person. It is strictly limited to those evenings alone in my kitchen. Once I start, there is this awful switch that flips. It's the strangest, most terrifying feeling, honestly. I can literally be sitting there, staring at the counter, and my rational brain is still working—I'll be thinking, *Taylor, put it away. Just close the box, put the lid back on, walk away right now.* I am fully aware that I need to stop. 

But my hands... it's like they belong to someone else entirely. They just keep moving. They just keep opening containers and tearing into packages and pulling things out of bags, like I am not the one in charge at all. I'll just be sitting there, practically watching my own hands do this, feeling completely disconnected from my own physical movements. It’s so bizarre because I don't lose control like that anywhere else. Not when I'm dealing with a furious vendor on the phone, not when I'm driving in terrible traffic, nowhere. It is only ever in those moments with the food, where that switch flips and I am suddenly just a passenger in my own body.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences loss of control over eating despite attempts to resist, which is key to differentiating between F50.2 (Binge Eating Disorder) and F50.9 (Eating Disorder, Unspecified).
doctor.question: During these episodes, even though you feel out of control, do you feel like you could stop if you really tried, or does it feel like you physically can't stop yourself once you start?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start, there is this awful switch that flips where I can be thinking, Taylor, put it away, and my hands still keep opening containers like I am not the one in charge.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking whether the patient feels they cannot stop eating once they start, which directly maps to the 'Loss of Control' symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying a moment ago about that awful switch flipping... it really feels like a physical impossibility to stop. You ask if I could stop if I really tried, and, doctor, I do try. I try so incredibly hard. I sit there at the kitchen island, and I am practically screaming at myself in my own head. I will be sitting there thinking, Taylor, put it away, just stop right now, you know exactly how you're going to feel tomorrow morning when your alarm goes off. 

But it is exactly like I was just trying to explain—my hands just keep opening the containers anyway. It is like there is a complete and total disconnect between my brain and my body. I will be holding one of those plastic takeout boxes, maybe the lo mein or the dumplings from the place down the street, and my rational mind is saying to put it in the fridge and walk away, but my fingers are already prying the lid off. 

It is terrifying, honestly. Because I am trying, I really am trying with every ounce of willpower I have left after a long day at the office, but it is like my body is completely overridden. I am just not the one in charge anymore once that first bite happens. I physically cannot make my hands stop bringing the food to my mouth or tearing open the next package, no matter how much I am begging myself to just put it away. It is just this relentless momentum, and I just have to ride it out until the food is gone, because I absolutely cannot stop myself once it starts.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of awareness or dissociation outside of the eating episodes, which could help differentiate between F50.2 (Binge Eating Disorder) and F50.9 (Eating Disorder, Unspecified).
doctor.question: Outside of these eating episodes, have you ever experienced any other moments where you felt disconnected from yourself or like you were not in control of your body?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about dissociative symptoms or loss of control outside of eating episodes, which is not covered by the Binge-Eating Disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, never. I know I sort of just touched on this, but it really is exclusively with the food. You would think if someone has this... this bizarre disconnect, it would happen in other stressful situations, right? But I don't have that at all. 

Like, just last Tuesday at the office, we had this massive crisis. Our main scheduling software went down right before a huge quarterly deadline, and my entire administrative team was in a total panic. I mean, people were practically running around like chickens with their heads cut off, some of the newer girls were practically in tears. And me? I was completely anchored. I just stood there in the middle of the bullpen, took a deep breath, and started delegating. I felt every bit in my body, completely present, totally in control of my actions and my words. I didn't freeze, I didn't feel like I was floating away or watching someone else do my job, like I do with the food. I was right there, handling it, just like I always do. 

I've been managing offices for years, and you just can't afford to lose yourself or disconnect when people are relying on you to keep the operations running smoothly. So, no, I've never experienced anything even remotely like that outside of my house. Everywhere else, I'm just regular, dependable, in-control Taylor. It is literally only when I have those wrappers and containers in front of me that I lose myself. So, to answer your question, no, absolutely not. Just the eating.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms align with binge-eating disorder, characterized by recurrent episodes of eating large quantities of food without compensatory behaviors, along with a sense of lack of control during the episodes. No other psychiatric or neurological dissociative symptoms were endorsed outside of the eating episodes, ruling out broader dissociative or other impulse control disorders.
